title: Successive Relearning
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Clark uses a single meta-analytic finding to correct a piece of professional development orthodoxy about how retrieval practice should be scheduled. He defines successive relearning, Rawson and Dunlosky's term, as retrieval repeated to a criterion, where the same content has to be correctly recalled on two or three separate occasions before a teacher counts it as learned. Against that he sets the expanding schedule that most retrieval training recommends, in which each gap is deliberately longer than the last. Drawing on Latimier, Peyre and Ramus's 2021 pooling of 29 studies, he reports a large benefit for spacing over massing and essentially no difference between expanding and uniform schedules. His explanation for why the expanding version feels better is that each attempt lands as memory fades, so the effort itself is mistaken for effectiveness. The practical half of the piece converts this into a classroom routine built on a fixed rota and a running tally of successful whole class retrievals rather than a calendar of review dates. He also flags a 2024 replication across nine university courses where the benefit varied widely, which keeps the claim from hardening into a guarantee.
points: The piece turns on a specific null result, that pooled across 29 studies an expanding gap schedule performed no better than a uniform one, with an effect size of 0.034.
It preserves the large finding alongside the null one, since spacing retrieval rather than massing it produced an effect size of 0.74 in the same meta-analysis.
Clark diagnoses the appeal of expanding schedules as a fluency illusion, where the extra effort of a later attempt is read as evidence that the schedule is working.
His operational fix is to count successful whole class retrievals per topic instead of scheduling review dates, because a tally survives disruption and reteaching while a term plan does not.
He caps the claim by citing a 2024 study across nine university courses where the same spaced quizzing design helped substantially in some subjects and barely at all in others.
quotes: Successive relearning is Katherine Rawson and John Dunlosky's term for a simple rule: students have to correctly retrieve the same content on two or three separate occasions, spaced days apart, before you count it as learned.
It's retrieval practice and spacing combined into one routine, rather than two good ideas you happen to be doing separately.

Most PD on this topic recommends a specific version of spacing: start with a short gap, then make each one bigger than the last. That's called an expanding schedule, and it's what most retrieval PD decks show you.
Results from subset 2 indicated no significant difference between expanding and uniform spacing schedules of retrieval practice (g = 0.034).
Results from subset 1 indicated a strong benefit of spaced retrieval practice in comparison with massed retrieval practice (g = 0.74).

It’s easy to see why expanding schedules feel more effective. Each retrieval attempt lands right as the last one is starting to fade, so it feels harder and more effortful — which is usually a decent proxy for "this is working." But a schedule feeling more effortful and a schedule producing better long-term retention turned out to be two different things.

The objection to all of this is obvious: nobody has time to individually track when every student last correctly retrieved every topic. The point of successive relearning as a classroom routine is that you don’t need to — you need a rota, not a spreadsheet.
A running tally — this topic has had zero, one, two correct whole-class retrievals — tells you what’s actually due next regardless of what the calendar says.
